summary.text: A discrete variable has a gap around each value it can take, so it has either a finite or a countably infinite number of permitted values.
Common examples are variables that must be integers, non-negative integers, positive integers, or only 0 and 1.
Their probability distributions can be expressed with probability mass functions, and calculus methods do not readily suit them.

facts.label: Permitted values
facts.value: Finite, or countably infinite in number

facts.label: Common examples
facts.value: Integers, or only the values 0 and 1

items.prompt: You count the cars in a parking lot at the top of each hour. Why is that count a discrete variable?

options.label: Each allowed count has a gap around it, with no allowed value between 3 and 4
It can be written down to as many decimal places as you like
It only ever takes small numbers, so it never gets very large
It changes from one hour to the next as time passes

items.explain: A variable is discrete when there is a positive distance to the nearest other permitted value. Whole-number counts fit that.

items.prompt: A researcher gives a person the value 0 if they are in the control group and 1 otherwise. What job does this 0-1 coding do in an equation?

options.label: It measures how far each person is from the group average
It acts as a switch that turns a parameter on or off
It rounds each person's results to the nearest whole number
It shows how many people are in each group

items.explain: A variable allowed only the values 0 and 1 is called a dummy variable, and it works as a switch that assigns two values to different parameters.

items.prompt: A statistician wants to write down the probability of each possible number of customers who walk in on an hour. Which kind of function fits?

options.label: A probability density function
A difference equation
A probability mass function
A differential equation

items.explain: Probability distributions of discrete variables are expressed with probability mass functions. Density functions are for continuous variables.

items.prompt: A savings account is updated once a day, and time is counted in whole days. What kind of equation describes how the balance evolves?

options.label: A differential equation
A probit equation
An instantaneous-rate equation
A difference equation

items.explain: When time is treated as discrete, the evolution of a variable is described by a difference equation. A differential equation goes with time treated as continuous.

items.prompt: A factory can buy only whole machines, never fractions of one. Which kind of problem is choosing how many to buy?

options.label: Integer programming
Continuous optimization
A problem about an instantaneous rate
A problem about a differential equation

items.explain: A variable restricted to integers is discrete, and integer programming is an example of a problem with discrete variables. Continuous optimization is for continuous ones.

items.prompt: A study measures each person with a yes/no symptom check and also with a smooth cognitive score. How are the two variables classed?

options.label: Both are discrete, because the symptom check is
The yes/no check is discrete and the score is continuous
Both are continuous, because the score is
The yes/no check is continuous and the score is discrete

items.explain: A binary measure is discrete and a cognitive performance score is continuous, so this is an example of a mixed model.

pack.title: Counting versus measuring
pack.question: What makes a variable discrete rather than continuous?

beats.title: Counting versus measuring
beats.hook: Some quantities leap from value to value with nothing in between, and that changes which maths you can use on them.

beats.prompt: A variable can be exactly 2 or exactly 3, and nothing in between. Is it continuous or discrete?
beats.explain: There is a non-infinitesimal gap around each value with no permitted values, so it is discrete around those values.

choices.label: Continuous, because 2 and 3 are real numbers
choices.feedback: Being a real number is not enough: a continuous variable needs possible values between any two of its values, and here there are none between 2 and 3.

choices.label: Discrete, because there is a gap on each side of each value
Continuous, because it has two end values to stop at
choices.feedback: Having end values does not make a variable continuous. What counts is whether values exist between any two permitted values.

beats.prompt: match each situation to the tool that goes with it
beats.explain: Each kind of variable, and each treatment of time, has its own matching description.

left.label: Any value in a range of the real numbers

beats.explain: Continuous variables can take any value in a range; discrete ones have separated permitted values such as integers.

steps.text: A variable can take only the values 0 and 1.
So there is a gap on each side of each value.
That makes it a discrete variable.
So calculus methods are the natural tool for it.

beats.explain: Calculus methods do not readily lend themselves to problems with discrete variables; they are often used for continuous ones.

beats.idea: A discrete variable has a gap around each permitted value, and its probabilities are described by mass functions rather than densities.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of quantity
paragraphs.text: A quantity that is measured by a number can be one of two kinds: continuous or discrete. A continuous variable can take two values and every value lying between them, so there is always another possibility in between. A discrete variable works differently. Around each value it can take, there is a gap of real size on both sides holding no allowed values. Some variables are even discrete over one stretch of the number line and continuous over another.

paragraphs.heading: Counting the allowed values
paragraphs.text: Another way to say it: a variable is discrete exactly when its values can be paired off, one to one, with some of the natural numbers. For any allowed value, there is a smallest positive distance to the next allowed one. The count of allowed values is either finite or countably infinite. Typical cases are variables that must be whole numbers, non-negative whole numbers, positive whole numbers, or just 0 and 1.

paragraphs.heading: Why the difference matters
paragraphs.text: In statistics the two kinds count as separate data types, and each is described by its own sort of probability distribution. For a discrete variable, the distribution can be written as a probability mass function; for a continuous one, as a probability density function. Calculus is often used when variables are continuous, but it does not fit problems with discrete variables so easily. Integer programming is one kind of problem built on discrete variables.

paragraphs.heading: Time in steps
paragraphs.text: Time itself can be treated either way. When time flows continuously, the equation for how something changes over time is a differential equation. When time moves in separate steps, that equation is called a difference equation instead. For some discrete-time systems, the difference equation can be solved for an analytical solution that models how the system responds.

paragraphs.heading: The 0-1 switch
paragraphs.text: A variable allowed only the values 0 and 1 is called a dummy variable. It acts like a switch, turning parts of an equation on or off by giving the two values to different parameters. In regression analysis it can mark subgroups of a sample, with 0 standing, for instance, for someone in the control group. When the outcome being predicted is itself a dummy variable, logistic or probit regression is the usual choice.

paragraphs.heading: When both kinds mix
paragraphs.text: Some models hold both kinds at once, such as a variable x that is only 0 or 1 next to a continuous variable y. A single random variable can be mixed too, and waiting in a queue is an example. The chance of waiting no time at all is a discrete piece, while any wait longer than zero is measured on a continuous time scale. The cumulative distribution function of such a mixed variable is neither purely discrete nor continuous everywhere.
